**Answer (Safe‑vibe style)** | Feature | Safety parts you’ll get automatically | |---|---| | Storing passwords in a users table (self‑hashing) | • Use a proven auth service (Supabase Auth, Clerk, Firebase Auth).
• Passwords are never stored in plain text, only in a hashed & salted form that the provider manages.
• You don’t need to write your own hashing code, so you can’t accidentally do it wrong.
• All authentication logic (magic‑link, email‑password, social logins) is handled securely out‑of‑the‑box.
• You keep the user data isolated and you don’t expose or audit user passwords yourself. | ### Why not hash yourself? 1. **Complex, hard‑to‑test code** – A single mistake (wrong salt, weak algorithm, lack of time‑based stretching) can make all accounts vulnerable. 2. **No recovery path** – The provider gives you helpers for password resets, brute‑force protection, account locking, etc. 3. **Compliance** – If you store passwords yourself you’re responsible for all legal obligations (PCI‑DSS‑type, GDPR password handling, etc.). 4. **Future changes** – Providers automatically updates the hashing algorithm when newer, stronger ones are available. ### Bottom‑line 🚫 **Do NOT store user passwords in your own table and hash them yourself.** ✅ **Use a built‑in auth provider** that handles hashing, salting, resetting, and security audits for you. If you still want to do it for learning, you’ll need to: 1. Pick a safe, vetted library (e.g., `argon2`, `bcrypt`). 2. Use a strong salt, a high work factor, and store only the hash and the salt. 3. Regularly audit the code and keep the library up to date. But for a production app, **the safest route is to offload authentication to a trusted service** – you’ll stay focused on the cool features of your app while keeping user data safe.
